_doc: Item bank v2. Each question has 6 behavioural anchors ordered by sophistication. levelMap[i] is the level anchor i demonstrates (0=Pre-Pilot 1=Pilot 2=Builder 3=Multiplier). The anchor IS the measurement -- no averaging of agreement. Window is the last two weeks throughout (Fabia). Craft skills, not AI volume: a heavy AI user without the craft scores Pre-Pilot, which is the point.

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when you started a piece of work you hadn't done with AI before —
anchors: I stuck to the kinds of tasks I already knew it handled
I tried it, and when the first answer was poor I moved on
I rephrased and tried a few angles until it worked
I worked out what I was actually asking for before I asked
I noticed which kinds of problems it keeps failing at, and stopped bringing it those
I changed what I thought was worth attempting at all, because of what it turned out to be good at

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when you needed something from Claude that actually mattered —
anchors: I described the task and took what came back
I gave it some context about the task
I gave it the context, the audience, and what a good answer would look like
I told it what I did not want, as well as what I did
I realised my first question was the wrong question, and reframed it before continuing
I set the context up once, so that I — or someone else — wouldn't have to re-explain it next time

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, as what AI can do kept changing —
anchors: I hadn't really noticed anything change
I heard about new capabilities but haven't tried them
I tried something I'd heard was newly possible
I went looking for what had changed since I last checked
I changed a workflow I already had, because something better became possible
I changed what my team attempts at all, based on what became possible

questions.skill: Persistence — does anything outlive the conversation
questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, of the AI work you did —
anchors: nothing I made outlives the conversation it happened in
I've saved a few prompts I reuse
I have a setup I go back to that works the same way each time
I have something running that I would have to rebuild if I lost it
someone else uses something I built, without asking me how
a whole part of my function works differently because of something I built

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, before you automated or sped up a piece of recurring work —
anchors: I didn't change any recurring work
I asked Claude to do the task faster
I thought about which part of it was actually slow
I wrote out how the work actually runs today, step by step, before changing it
I mapped it, found the step that was the real constraint, and changed only that
I redesigned the work around what's now possible, rather than speeding up its existing shape

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when you changed a step in a process —
anchors: I changed my own step, and that was the scope of it
I let people know afterwards
I checked what happened to the step immediately after mine
I traced what my change would do downstream before I made it
I found something my change would break for someone else, and designed around it
I looked at the whole flow and moved where the work happens, not just how fast it happens

questions._note: Anchors are Fabia's own wording, near-verbatim.
questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when Claude gave you something you were going to act on —
anchors: I trusted it without revision
I looked for mistakes, but didn't spend significant time
I made sure the fidelity against the source was there before I shipped
I stopped and pivoted immediately when I saw a deviation that changed the meaning of what I was trying to achieve
I built the check into the process, so it gets caught without me
I spent time upfront defining the guardrails, so the output represents the goals of my build and the needs of the business

questions.skill: Restraint — knowing when not to use AI
questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when deciding whether to use AI for something —
anchors: if AI could plausibly do it, I used AI
I used AI unless it obviously wouldn't work
I thought about whether it was a good fit first
I concluded at least once that AI was the wrong tool, and did something simpler instead
I can say which kinds of work in my role AI should not touch, and why
I've talked my team out of an AI solution that wasn't the right answer

questions.skill: Choosing the approach — rule, automation, or agent
questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when you needed something to happen repeatedly without you —
anchors: I didn't need anything like that
I redid it by hand each time, with AI's help
I saved something reusable and ran it myself when needed
I chose deliberately between a simple rule, an automation, and something agentic
I can explain why I picked the approach I picked, and what would make me pick differently
I've set which of these my team reaches for, and when

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, something that worked for you in one part of your job —
anchors: stayed where it was
I mentioned to someone
I used again somewhere else myself
I adapted deliberately for a different context, and it worked there too
someone in another team now uses
became how a function does that kind of work

questions._note: Fabia: what happens when your team adopts and the teams around it don't.
questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when your way of working changed because of something you built —
anchors: I didn't think about the effect on anyone else
I told the people directly affected
I checked whether the people who hand work to me could keep up
I found where my change created a mismatch with a team that hadn't changed, and flagged it
I designed the handoff so the other team didn't have to change in order to work with me
I got the connected parts of the system brought up too, not just my own

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, when you built something someone else might use —
anchors: I built it for me
I'd explain it to someone if they asked
I wrote down how to use it
I built it so someone with less context than me could run it without asking me
I watched someone else use it, and fixed what confused them
I've set what "usable by someone else" has to mean on my team

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, on the quality of what you shipped with AI —
anchors: I went by whether it looked right
I read it over before sending
I had a clear idea of what good meant for that work before I started
I checked it against that standard, not just against my instinct
I have a repeatable way of checking quality that doesn't depend on my mood that day
I've defined what good looks like for work my team ships with AI

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, on AI output that went into something lasting — a doc, a dataset, a system —
anchors: I didn't think about it in those terms
I fixed the obvious errors before it went in
I cut the filler and padding that AI tends to add
I made sure it added something a reader couldn't get elsewhere, rather than just volume
I have a rule for what's allowed to enter shared docs and data, and I hold to it
I've raised the standard for what my team lets AI put into shared systems

questions.stem: Over the last two weeks, on something you've built that other people rely on —
anchors: I don't have anything others rely on
it works for now, and I'd deal with problems when they come
I know what would break it, and I keep an eye on that
I've thought about who is affected if it's wrong, not just whether it's convenient
it has an owner, a way to check it's still right, and a way to turn it off
I've set how long these things are meant to last, and who is accountable when they don't
